quote: (a) Kubient agrees to indemnify, defend, and hold harmless Customer and its officers, directors, managers, members, agents, and employees from all third-party allegations, claims, actions, losses, expenses, damages, costs (including, without limitation, reasonable attorneys' fees) or liabilities ("Claims") arising out of or in connection with:
rationale: Section 10(a) gives us a broad Vendor defend/indemnify/hold-harmless obligation covering third-party Claims arising out of the Services, the Auction Platform, the Creative, Kubient's breach of any representation or warranty, and the acts or omissions of Kubient and its subcontractors. Because Kubient's warranties expressly include non-infringement of third-party IP (§9(b)(i): "the Service and any deliverables provided hereunder by Kubient do not and shall not infringe, misappropriate or violate any patent, copyright, trademark, trade secret, publicity, privacy or other rights of any third party"), data security (§9(b)(iii)) and compliance with Law (§9(b)(v), (ix)), the IP-infringement, breach-of-law, data-breach and misconduct heads of the preferred position are all captured, with no infringement carve-outs. Section 11 supplies the standard procedure (prompt notice that is not a condition precedent, indemnitor control of defence and settlement subject to no admission of liability against us, cooperation at the indemnitor's cost), and §7(a) carves indemnification out of the consequential-damages exclusion, so no super-cap constrains recovery. This sits at (indeed above) the preferred position. Two sub-elements short of the ideal are noted but not flagged: our reciprocal indemnity in §10(b) reaches our breach of any representation or warranty and our acts or omissions rather than being confined to Content/Properties and breach of law, and the §10(a)(iii) Creative head is knowledge-qualified. Both are mutual-drafting artefacts that do not defeat the Vendor indemnity rule, and the Customer-side breadth is better addressed under the customer-indemnity rule than by reopening this clause.

quote: (h) Neither Party may assign (voluntarily, by operation of law, or otherwise) this Agreement or any rights or obligations under this Agreement without the other Party's prior written consent, which shall not be unreasonably withheld, provided however, that either Party may assign this Agreement without approval or consent to any affiliate or purchaser of all or substantially all of said Party's assets related to the subject matter of this Agreement or to any successor by way of merger, stock sale, consolidation or similar transaction.
rationale: The assignment clause in § (h) gives AP (and Kubient) the right to assign without consent to an affiliate, to a purchaser of all or substantially all relevant assets, or to a successor by merger, stock sale or consolidation, with all other assignments subject to consent that may not be unreasonably withheld. That is the mutual successor-assignment/reasonable-consent structure of our fallback position, and the M&A carve-out we require for AP is expressly present. There is no change-of-control provision anywhere in the document, so Kubient has no termination or re-pricing right on an AP change of control (searches for "change of control" and "merger" return nothing else). Short of the preferred position only in two minor respects — the consent restriction is symmetrical rather than one-way, and there is no express bar on assignment to an AP competitor — which we note but do not redline. The "non-transferable, non-assignable" language in the § 2 license grant is a scope-of-licence limitation, not an assignment restriction, and is governed by § (h).

rationale: The grant in paragraph 2 is expressly "revocable" with no qualification, so on its face Kubient may revoke at its discretion (paragraph 4(c)(ii) only confirms revocation on termination; it does not limit revocation to that event). quote: Either Party may terminate this Agreement for any reason following the Initial Term upon ninety (90) days written notice to the other Party.
rationale:
Compliant at the playbook fallback; no redline and no counterparty-facing comment. Reconciling the failed deterministic check first: the check searches for literal "for convenience" wording and therefore misses this clause's formulation, "terminate this Agreement for any reason." A right to terminate "for any reason" is a termination-for-convenience right — it requires no cause, breach, or trigger — so the failure is a phrasing variant, not a missing right. No substantive defect was identified on re-review.

Material terms against T4C: (1) Customer convenience right is present — AP may terminate "for any reason" following the Initial Term on ninety (90) days' written notice, sitting at the outer edge of the fallback's 60–90 day notice window. (2) Term structure — a one (1) year Initial Term with 1-year automatic renewals, so the detection trigger for "absence of any Customer convenience right in a term longer than 12 months" is not met and there is no multi-year lock-in; AP holds a rolling 90-day exit from the end of year one onward. (3) The mid-Initial-Term bar ("Neither Party may terminate this Agreement during the Initial Term") is symmetric and equally prevents Kubient from walking away on AP mid-term, so it operates partly in our favour and is not flagged against us. (4) No early-termination fee or penalty falls on AP — Kubient is entitled only to fees "generated during the termination period," i.e. revenue actually earned while it continues performing across the 90-day notice period, which is within the fallback's 3-months'-fees ceiling. (5) Kubient's convenience right arises only after the Initial Term and on exactly ninety (90) days' notice — not "fewer than 90 days" — so it stays outside walk-away territory.

Sub-elements short of the preferred position, noted rather than escalated per the playbook's classification semantics: 90-day rather than 30-day notice; Kubient's right not confined to the end of a renewal term; and no pro-rata refund of prepaid fees, which is inapplicable because §5 (p0023) is a revenue-share under which funds flow from Kubient to AP within seven (7) days of receipt, so AP prepays no fees capable of refund.

verification.notes: Customer convenience termination present: failed Claimed status is compliant with no redline and no counterparty comment, which is the expected output shape for a clause sitting at the fallback; nothing was proposed that could over-flag or mis-edit the text. The cited text supports the classification: §4(a) gives either Party a no-cause right ('terminate this Agreement for any reason') after a 1-year Initial Term on ninety (90) days' notice, which lands inside the fallback's 60–90 day Customer notice window and outside walk-away territory (Vendor notice is exactly 90 days, not fewer). The T4C detection trigger for a missing Customer convenience right requires a committed term longer than 12 months; the Initial Term is exactly one year with 1-year auto-renewals, and the mid-Initial-Term bar is symmetric (it equally locks Kubient in), so it is not adverse to us. No early-termination penalty is imposed on the Customer — Kubient is entitled only to fees 'generated during the termination period' (i.e., earned while performing through the 90-day notice), well within the fallback's 3-months'-fees ceiling, and the revenue-share structure means the Customer prepays no refundable fees. The failed deterministic check is credibly reconciled: the regex looks for literal 'for convenience' wording and misses the equivalent 'for any reason' formulation, so it is a phrasing variant rather than a substantive gap. Residual gaps (90-day rather than 30-day Customer notice, no pro-rata prepaid-fee refund, and Kubient's convenience right not confined to the end of a renewal term) are correctly recorded as sub-elements short of the preferred position rather than escalated; the last of these is the closest call, but with 90 days' notice and a rolling 1-year term it does not defeat the fallback on a material term.

quote: The relationship of the Parties is that of independent contractors, and nothing herein is intended, nor should be construed, to create a partnership, agency, joint venture or employment relationship.
rationale:
The Agreement contains no non-solicitation, no-hire or anti-poaching covenant, so nothing restricts the Customer's hiring freedom. Targeted searches for "solicit", "non-solicitation", "induce", "recruit", "hire", "employ", "personnel", "covenant" and "restrict" surface only: indemnity references to third parties "hired by, employed, retained or under" a party's control (p0051, p0052); confidentiality permissions to disclose to employees and directors (p0061); the consequential-damages carve-out (p0027); data-security references to "authorized personnel" (p0035, p0045); representations and warranties styled as "covenants" (p0029-p0032); the non-exclusivity statement, which operates in our favour (p0001); and the waiver clause (p0070). The miscellaneous provisions (p0064-p0068: governing law, publicity, independent contractors, fees, notices) - the usual home for such a covenant - contain none. The cited p0066 imposes no hiring restriction and is referenced only as the location marker where a non-solicit would ordinarily sit.

This meets the rule's preferred position ("No non-solicit on Customer") outright. Because the rule targets a restriction imposed on us, absence is full compliance rather than a "missing" clause; treating it as missing would wrongly imply we should ask Kubient to insert a covenant constraining our own hiring. No redline and no comment are warranted.

The deterministic sub-checks for a 12-month duration limit and a general-solicitation carve-out register as failed only because there is no non-solicit clause whose scope, term or carve-outs could be measured. Read as heuristics rather than verdicts, they are artifacts of absence and do not undermine the finding. If Kubient introduces a non-solicit in negotiation, we would hold it to the fallback: mutual, limited to personnel directly involved in the services, 12 months from the end of their involvement, with carve-outs for general advertisements and unsolicited approaches, and no no-hire.

rationale: The effects-of-termination clause (paragraph 4(c)) addresses only cessation of the Services, revocation of the licence, and each Party's return or destruction of the other's Confidential Information. There is no transition-assistance obligation, no obligation to return or export our data (Content, Requests, reporting and visitor data held by Kubient) in a usable format, and no deletion certification; nothing elsewhere in the Agreement supplies these. That fails even the fallback (90 days' assistance plus a 30-day export), and the current "return or destroy" election lets Kubient unilaterally destroy our data on termination, which is walk-away territory. We therefore insert the preferred transition, machine-readable return within 30 days, and certified deletion language into paragraph 4(c).

quote: (ix) it is now and throughout the Term shall comply with all applicable Laws in connection with the operation of its business and the performance of its obligations hereunder or the provision of the Service
rationale:
Compliant, at or above the preferred position. Section 9(b) is a live express warranty package from Kubient: the Service "will perform in all material respects to industry standards" (p0034); services "shall comply with the terms of this Agreement and shall be free from errors that materially affect their utility" (p0038); the product and service "shall be free of any viruses, Trojan Horses, worms, time bombs, trap doors, back doors" and similar routines (p0036); and Kubient "is now and throughout the Term shall comply with all applicable Laws" (p0041). That covers the preferred position's substantive elements — professional/industry-standard performance, material conformance, no malicious code, and compliance with laws.

On duration: the warranties in 9(b) are framed as continuing representations, warranties and covenants ("will perform", "shall be free from errors", "throughout the Term") rather than as a fixed post-delivery window. There is therefore no explicit "90 days" or "12 months" figure to extract, which is why a period-matching check reports nothing; this is a drafting-form artifact, not a shortfall. A warranty running for the entire Term (one-year Initial Term with automatic one-year renewals under 4(a)) is longer and better for us than the preferred 12-month/90-day parameters, so no extension is needed and inserting a fixed period would risk shortening our protection.

On the disclaimer: Section 13 (p0062) is double-carved — "Except as expressly set forth herein" and "except for the representations and warranties set forth in this Agreement" — so the "as is" language reaches only implied warranties (merchantability, fitness, course of dealing) and the no-minimum-revenue acknowledgement. The express warranty survives intact and the clause is nowhere near walk-away "AS IS" territory.

Noted but not flagged: there is no express repair / re-performance / refund remedy sentence. That is a sub-element short of the preferred wording rather than a material failure, and its absence favours us — with no exclusive-remedy or monetary cap, we retain full direct-damages recovery, indemnity for breach of warranty (p0051), and the right to terminate on 30 days' uncured material breach (p0016). Adding an exclusive remedy would narrow our rights, so no redline is proposed.
